messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rohan still remembers the smell of burnt rubber and pavement that day his car was pulled over by a police officer. The officer's tone was aggressive, and Rohan felt a surge of fear as he tried to explain that he had done nothing wrong. But before he could finish speaking, the officer cut him off and began yelling at him. Rohan recalls feeling a wave of guilt wash over him, as if he must have somehow deserved this treatment. When he catches a whiff of something burning, even years later, Rohan is instantly transported back to that moment. The smell triggers a flood of memories, including the officer's angry face and the feeling of helplessness that followed. He can't shake the sense that people in uniform are inherently untrustworthy - that they're just waiting for an excuse to pounce. As a result, Rohan has become hypervigilant around anyone who looks like they might be in authority, constantly scanning their surroundings for potential threats. Rohan's difficulty articulating what happened that day is another source of distress. He knows what occurred, but whenever he tries to put it into words, the memories feel jumbled and unclear. This has led him to rehearse conversations in his head before any interaction, hoping to avoid feeling tongue-tied or defensive. Avoiding future plans has also become a habit - why make commitments when the world is just waiting to let you down? When Rohan does try to explain what happened, he often feels like he's losing the thread and can't finish. As time passes, these patterns of thought have only intensified. Rohan has come to believe that people are inherently untrustworthy, and that the world is a fundamentally dangerous place. He feels betrayed by the very system that's supposed to protect him - after all, who else was there to turn to when he needed help? This sense of betrayal fuels his hypervigilance, making it harder for him to distinguish between real threats and imagined ones. Lately, Rohan has noticed that even his work as a graphic designer is being affected. He used to love brainstorming with colleagues, but now the mere presence of authority figures in the office makes him anxious. His avoidance behaviors have started to take a toll on his relationships - his wife feels like he's pushing her away, and friends are starting to notice that Rohan never wants to make plans anymore. Rohan knows this can't go on forever. He's hoping therapy will help him untangle these knotted thoughts and feelings, and maybe - just maybe - learn to trust again. But for now, the smell of burnt rubber still sends a shiver down his spine, transporting him back to that fateful day when everything changed.
